text:
For a submartingale, conditional order gives the reverse bound
\(E(E(X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n)\mid\mathcal G_n)\geq
E(X_n\mid\mathcal G_n)=X_n\). For a martingale,
\(E(X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n)=X_n\) almost surely, so the tower identity
gives \(E(X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal G_n)=E(X_n\mid\mathcal G_n)=X_n\).
Both cases, and their derivation from the supermartingale case through
\(X\mapsto-X\), are written in \cref{annex:p15-w02c-p15-019-reduced-filtration}.
Integrability is unchanged, and adaptedness
was explicitly assumed.

text:
Summing yields \(\int_AX_T\,dP\leq\int_AX_S\,dP\) for every
\(A\in\mathcal F_S\).
Since \(X_S\) is integrable and \(\mathcal F_S\)-measurable, the
event-comparison lemma \cref{thm:p15-w02c-p15-019-event-comparison}
then proves \(E(X_T\mid\mathcal F_S)\leq X_S\): on each test event
\(\{E(X_T\mid\mathcal F_S)-X_S>1/r\}\in\mathcal F_S\) the integral of the
difference is at most zero and at least the event's probability over \(r\).
For a martingale every term is zero, giving the defining identity
and equality by uniqueness.
For a submartingale each term has nonnegative expectation, the event
integrals satisfy \(\int_AX_T\,dP\geq\int_AX_S\,dP\), and the same
lemma gives \(E(X_T\mid\mathcal F_S)\geq X_S\); this case is written in
\cref{annex:p15-w02c-p15-019-sampling-cases}.

and the event that the sequence has a finite limit, where both are

anchor_quote:
If the bracket were negative on a set of positive probability, one
of its \(\mathcal F_n\)-events where it is at most \(-1/k\)

text:
The bracket is \(\mathcal F_n\)-measurable: the conditional expectation
is so by definition, and \(X_n\) is so because the submartingale is
adapted by hypothesis. For \(k\geq1\) the events
\(A_k=\{E(X_\infty\mid\mathcal F_n)-X_n\leq-1/k\}\) therefore belong to
\(\mathcal F_n\), and they increase to the event where the bracket is
negative. If that event had positive probability, some \(A_k\) would
have \(P(A_k)>0\), and then
\(\int_{A_k}[E(X_\infty\mid\mathcal F_n)-X_n]\,dP\leq-P(A_k)/k<0\),
contradicting the inequality just proved.

anchor_quote: \index{L\'evy zero-one law}
text:
The source names the first assertion L\'evy's 0-1 law
\cite[thm.~4.6.9, p.~247]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}. Opening with a line it
borrows from K.~L.~Chung, it asks whether the law is obvious or
incredible and argues both ways: obvious, because \(\mathbf1_A\) is
\(\mathcal F_\infty\)-measurable and \(\mathcal F_n\) increases to
\(\mathcal F_\infty\), so the best guess of \(\mathbf1_A\) from
\(\mathcal F_n\) should approach \(\mathbf1_A\); incredible, because
for a tail event of independent variables the same statement gives
Kolmogorov's 0-1 law. It closes by judging that this and later
applications show the theorem to be very useful
\cite[pp.~247--248]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}. Both readings are set out,
with each step proved, in \cref{def:p15-w02c-p15-014-levy-readings}.

text:
To identify its limit for a given closing variable \(Z\), take the
limit version constructed in the proof of the submartingale result,
which is measurable with respect to \(\mathcal F_\infty\). That
construction applies here: the martingale is adapted by hypothesis, so
each \(X_n\) is measurable with respect to \(\mathcal F_n\) and hence
with respect to \(\mathcal F_\infty\), and the event where the sequence
has a finite limit belongs to \(\mathcal F_\infty\).
